articles.title: Overshooting 1.5 Degrees Celsius: A Bleak Report - The University Times

articles.full_text:
A recent climate report was published by the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) in Nairobi on September 3rd, 2026. The report, entitled Limiting Overshoot, warns that global temperatures are likely to exceed the 1.5 degree Celsius limit agreed under the Paris Agreement in 2015. Even under an optimistic scenario based on current government commitments, warming could peak at around 1.8 degrees.
Although this report may seem alarming at first glance, we are also told that it is possible to reverse the situation by adopting an “Overshoot, peak and decline” plan to return to 1.5 degrees Celsius, or even lower if possible, although this is less likely.
The Executive Director of UNEP, Inger Andersen, even stated that “there will be no positive outcomes if we remain above 1.5 degrees Celsius.” Indeed, the report makes it clear that the consequences of exceeding this temperature threshold would include intensified extreme weather, ecosystem loss and the submersion of Small Island Developing States and low-lying coastal cities, whilst also affecting food security and human health.
ADVERTISEMENT
It could also increase the risk of irreversible changes, or “tipping points”, involving systems such as the Greenland and West Antarctic ice sheets, the Amazon rainforest and the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation. The report therefore states that we must undertake both mitigation and adaptation measures, and even utilise carbon dioxide removal to bring the temperature back down to 1.5 degrees, for example, by capturing CO2 from the air or restoring ecosystems.
Finally, the report emphasises the importance of climate equity. Countries have different levels of historical responsibility, resources, and vulnerability, meaning that climate action must take these differences into account. The report also stresses the need for greater international cooperation, climate finance, technology transfer and long-term governance, as managing climate overshoot and its consequences could take decades or even longer.

articles.full_text:
Representational photo
| Photo Credit: File Photo
Thunderstorms accompanied by lightning and gusty winds are active across Keralam ahead of the onset of the northeast monsoon. Large parts of the State, particularly the Ghat regions that form the principal rain-catchment area during the northeast monsoon, have been witnessing spells of heavy rain, thunderstorms, lightning and strong winds.
During the last 24 hours ending at 8.30 a.m. on Wednesday (October 7, 2026), Ranni in Pathanamthitta recorded the highest rainfall of 9 cm, followed by Thadiyoor in Pathanamthitta with 7 cm, Chittur in Palakkad, Laha in Pathanamthitta and Nooranad in Alapuzha with 6 cm each. According to a weather bulletin issued by the India Meteorological Department (IMD) on Wednesday, a trough from the Gulf of Mannar to Madhya Maharashtra now runs from the Gulf of Mannar to North Interior Karnataka across Tamil Nadu and south Interior Karnataka at 0.9 km above mean sea level.
Though the trade wind associated with the southwest monsoon has been weakened, the weather system over the Bay of Bengal has been triggering rainfall across the State by drawing moisture from both the Bay of Bengal and the Arabian Sea. The increased moisture is supporting cloud formation and fuelling rain and thunderstorms across the State. A yellow alert has been issued for Pathanamthitta, Kottayam, Idukki, Ernakulam and Malappuram districts on Thursday, warning of isolated heavy rains.
Published - October 07, 2026 06:44 pm IST

articles.full_text:
Rain and thunderstorms are likely to continue in major parts of Karnataka, as the India Meteorological Department (IMD) has issued a yellow alert for multiple districts on Wednesday, October 7.
The weather department has warned of thunderstorms and rainfall activity, mainly during the evening hours today while coastal Karnataka weather is expected to be rainy until October 10.
The districts under the yellow alert are Bengaluru Rural and Bengaluru Urban, Chikkamagaluru, Hassan, Shivamogga, Kodagu, Mandya, Mysuru, Chamarajanagar, Bengaluru Rural and Bengaluru Urban. The IMD forecast indicates the possibility of good rainfall in these areas, with residents advised to be cautious during thunderstorms.
Karnataka Weather Today
The coastal districts of Dakshina Kannada, Udupi and Uttara Kannada may receive light to moderate rainfall at some places, while showers are also possible in Ramanagara. The coastal belt is expected to remain relatively active, with scattered thunderstorms forecast through October 10.
Parts of the Malnad and South Interior Karnataka region are also likely to see scattered rainfall. However, rainfall activity over parts of the interior state is expected to gradually slow down from October 8.
Meanwhile, several parts of North Karnataka are expected to remain comparatively dry, including Bagalkot, Belagavi, Bidar, Dharwad, Gadag, Haveri, Kalaburagi, Koppal, Raichur, Vijayapura and Yadgir.
Bengaluru Weather Today
Bengaluru started Wednesday on a relatively pleasant note. According to the weather update by IMD, the city recorded a temperature of 22°C. The weather was partly sunny, with an ESE wind speed of 11 kmph and wind gusts of up to 13 kmph. The forecast indicates a high of 30°C during the day, with temperatures expected to fall to around 20°C at night.
The Bengaluru weather forecast also points to a possibility of thunderstorms during the afternoon. Bengaluru Urban is among the districts which are under the yellow alert today. This means residents should be prepared for a possible change in weather, particularly later in the day.
The Bengaluru rain may affect evening commuters, especially if thunderstorms comes with sudden showers which will eventually lead to waterlogging in low-lying areas.
The IMD's forecast for the city shows that evening thunderstorm activity could continue across parts of South Interior Karnataka for the next few days, even as overall rainfall activity is now weakened in some areas.

A dangerous, long-lasting heat wave continues through Thursday. Cooler Friday
Hot through Thursday, then a big trough of low pressure cools us down this weekend into the 60s and low 70s and introduces a robust marine layer cloud pattern
Here is your Central Coast Weather Outlook from Meteorologist Jim Castillo
Current Heat Wave Overview (Through Thursday)
A dangerous, long-lasting heat wave continues across San Luis Obispo and Santa Barbara Counties, including the Santa Lucia Mountains, Santa Ynez Mountains, and the Los Padres National Forest.
Coastal and interior valleys across the region will see extreme highs of 85 to 104 degrees, well above normal.
Even coastal beaches will offer little relief, with afternoon highs climbing into the 70s and 80s through Thursday.
Overnight lows will stay exceptionally warm, dropping only into the 60s in many areas.
Heat advisories and extreme heat warnings remain in effect through Thursday evening for all coastal zones, valleys, mountains, and inland sectors of San Luis Obispo and Santa Barbara counties.
The transition and cooling trend begins Friday and really cools off Saturday and Sunday.
The upper-level high-pressure system breaks down on Friday, replaced by weak cyclonic flow, lowering upper heights, establishing onshore flow to the east, and leaving only weak offshore flow from the north.
High temperatures on Friday will trend downward into the 80s and 90s across interior valleys; while still above normal, it will mark a transition out of dangerously hot levels.
A robust upper trough moves into California on Saturday, significantly increasing onshore flow and sparking the return of marine layer stratus clouds along the coast.
Weekend Tropical Moisture and Late-Week Swell
Moisture from distant Hurricane Rachel approaches Southern California by Sunday, staying mostly southeast of the Central Coast. That said, there is a 20% to 30% chance for showers on Monday for the Central Coast.
A big trough of low pressure cools us down this weekend into the 60s and low 70s and introduces a robust marine layer cloud pattern.
Additional cooling on Sunday will push maximum temperatures back down to normal or slightly below normal levels across San Luis Obispo and Santa Barbara counties.
Ocean impacts from the system will arrive soon after, with swells generated by Hurricane Rachel that could reach local waters by next week.
Find AC if at all possible and stay hydrated. We'll cool down by Friday!
